newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU tries to calm feed market with barley sale.
newsitem.headline: EU tries to calm feed market with barley sale.

text.p: The European Union acted cautiously on Thursday to calm concerns over a domestic glut of feed grain by quickly releasing some feed grain for export at the start of the new season, a European grain official said.
The official said the barley and rye sale was meant to calm an increasingly tough situation for domestic operators who face competition to sell a large and partly rain-spoiled crop.
"We are coming up to a difficult period for feed wheat so accepting the barley was one way of calming down the feed market," he said.
A symbolic 1,000 tonne rye export award would give much the same signal, he said.
The EU accepted bids at its first grain tender for 1997/98 (July/June) on Thursday to export 70,000 tonnes of barley from the free market at a maximum refund of 14.92 Ecus per tonne.
It granted 1,000 tonnes of rye at 23.19 Ecus.
Analysts valued the barley award at $124 fob France and $125 fob Germany, though in fact around two thirds of the barley will come from Finland which has a surplus from the last crop.
The rye was sold for $112 per tonne fob.

A near-record overall harvest of possibly 200 million tonnes, coupled with rain which has caused a variety of quality problems, threaten the EU with a big surplus of feed and a two-tier market for domestic grain this year.
Rainfall has caused early germination in the fields in parts of northern Europe, ruling the grain out for high-value food processing and brewing.
While few precise figures are available, malting barley supplies are already said to be scarce while few wheat sellers are prepared to guarantee the quality required for top milling.
Competing feed ingredients like corn gluten and manioc are also expected to be in heavy supply this year.
The official denied speculation that a separate decision to ease barley exports through the EU's alternative daily bidding channel was prompted specifically by current shipments to the Middle East.
The EU set a prefixable zero refund on barley sales taken out through the daily channel, replacing a volatile "nil value" licence in force previously.

The official said the EU had also made a routine decision to award a special 13-Ecu standing refund for barley sales to Switzlerand and Liechtenstein, and it was normal for the refund to other countries to be adjusted to the same rules.
